Speckled
SPEK-ld
adj.
From speckle, a small spot, from Saxon specca. Webster 1828: marked with small spots of a different colour. Scripture uses it of Laban’s flocks in the account of Jacob’s wages, of a bird set upon by others, and of the horses of Zechariah’s first vision.

Biblical Definition

Speckled means marked with spots of another colour, and its principal use is the strangest wage negotiation in Scripture. Jacob proposes to take as his hire only the irregular animals: I will pass through all thy flock to day, removing from thence all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown cattle among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and of such shall be my hire (Genesis 30:32). Laban changes the terms repeatedly, and Jacob later tells his wives how it went: If he said thus, The speckled shall be thy wages; then all the cattle bare speckled: and if he said thus, The ringstraked shall be thy hire; then bare all the cattle ringstraked (Genesis 31:8). Whatever Laban named, the flocks produced — and Jacob attributes it not to his rods in the watering troughs but to God, who hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me. Jeremiah uses the word of a nation marked out for attack: Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird, the birds round about are against her (Jeremiah 12:9). And Zechariah sees speckled horses among the patrol that walks the earth (Zechariah 1:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SPECKLED as marked with specks; variegated with spots of a different colour from the ground or surface.

expand to see more

SPECKLED, a. — Marked with specks; variegated with spots of a different colour from the ground.

SPECKLE, n. — A small spot in anything of a different substance or colour from that of the thing itself.

Applied in Scripture chiefly to cattle, goats, sheep, birds, and horses.

Distinguished from ringstraked, marked with rings or bands, and from spotted, marked with larger patches.

From Saxon specca, a spot — the root also of speck and speckle.

Key Scripture

Genesis 30:32 — "I will pass through all thy flock to day, removing from thence all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown cattle among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and of such shall be my hire."

Genesis 31:8 — "If he said thus, The speckled shall be thy wages; then all the cattle bare speckled: and if he said thus, The ringstraked shall be thy hire; then bare all the cattle ringstraked."

Jeremiah 12:9 — "Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird, the birds round about are against her; come ye, assemble all the beasts of the field, come to devour."

Zechariah 1:8 — "I saw by night, and behold a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom; and behind him were there red horses, speckled, and white."

Modern Corruption

The rods in the watering troughs are sometimes read as a piece of folk breeding-magic that Scripture endorses, when the narrative itself credits God and Jacob says so plainly to his wives.

expand to see more

Genesis 30 records what Jacob did — peeled rods of poplar, hazel and chestnut set in the gutters where the flocks came to drink — without saying it worked. Genesis 31 gives the explanation, and it comes from Jacob’s own mouth and from an angel in a dream: God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me, and the angel says I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee. Scripture frequently narrates what men did without endorsing it; the polygamy of the patriarchs is reported in the same manner. The lesson of the chapter is providence overruling a decade of a cheat’s manoeuvres — Laban changed Jacob’s wages ten times, and every change was answered from heaven before Jacob could think of a device.

Jeremiah 12:9 turns the image against God’s own people, and the pastoral point is worth naming. A speckled bird in a flock of plain ones is attacked by the rest for being unlike them, and God says His heritage has become such a bird. Judah’s distinctness, which should have been her glory as the people bearing God’s name, had become the mark that drew the beasts. The chapter is Jeremiah’s complaint that the wicked prosper and God’s answer that harder things are coming — if thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? A church distinct from its neighbours should expect the treatment of the speckled bird, and should not conclude from it that God has abandoned His heritage.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew naqod (H5348), speckled, marked with points; taluw (H2921), spotted; aqod (H6124), ringstraked, banded; tsabua (H6641), coloured, speckled — the word of Jeremiah 12:9.

expand to see more

Hebrew naqod (H5348) — speckled, marked with points; the term of Jacob’s wages (Genesis 30:32).

Hebrew aqod (H6124) — ringstraked, marked with bands at the ankles; the alternative Laban proposed.

Hebrew taluw (H2921) — spotted, patched; the third category in the same negotiation.

Hebrew tsabua (H6641) — coloured, variegated; as a speckled bird (Jeremiah 12:9).

Hebrew barod (H1261) — grisled, dappled; the speckled horses of Zechariah 1:8 and 6:3.

Usage

"Of such shall be my hire (Genesis 30:32) — a wage taken only from the irregular animals."

"If he said thus, The speckled shall be thy wages; then all the cattle bare speckled (Genesis 31:8) — every change of terms answered from heaven."

"Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird (Jeremiah 12:9) — distinctness that draws the flock’s attack."
